Prints '1 2' if both constants exist; if only the first survived, B would be an undefined name and the module would fail to compile rather than print something wrong -- so this case cannot silently pass on half the line.

Why: Two Declare statements colon-joined at module level. Harder than the Const case because a Declare ends with an argument list and an optional As clause, so the parser must decide the statement is finished at the closing paren before it can treat the colon as a separator rather than as part of the signature. Two Deftype statements joined by a colon. These are the most position-sensitive lines in a module -- VB6 has a dedicated error for a Deftype appearing after declarations -- so they are the best test of whether the colon is understood before or after the compiler decides which section of the module it is reading. Fully observable: prints 'Integer String' only if both ranges were installed, and 'Integer Variant' if the half after the colon was lost.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 0 : Expected: statement or end of statement Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: A colon that would have to open a procedure definition rather than merely separate two statements. Predicted illegal on a structural argument, not a lexical one: VB6 splits a module into procedures before compiling any of them -- this is why the VBE can display one procedure at a time -- and that split is by physical line, so a Sub header sharing a line with a preceding declaration has nowhere to start. Distinct from the declaration joins above in exactly one respect: what follows the colon is a block header, not a statement.

An entire procedure -- header, body and terminator -- on one physical line. Genuinely unsure and worth measuring: the lexical view says these are three ordinary statements separated by colons, while the structural view above says a procedure boundary is a property of the physical line. Prints IN if the whole line compiled, so a legal result also confirms the body ran rather than being parsed and discarded. If this is legal but the previous case is not, the rule is 'a procedure must START a line', not 'a procedure must own its lines'.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 2 : Syntax error Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: The other half of the procedure-boundary question: a colon joining one procedure's terminator to the next one's header. Predicted illegal for the same by-physical-line splitting reason. Worth having alongside the previous two because it is the shape a code generator or minifier most plausibly emits, and because it fails in a different place -- the colon sits between two procedures rather than inside or before one.

A Type member split by a continuation between the member name and its As clause. Predicted legal because continuations are resolved by the scanner, below the level at which the Type block's member syntax is recognised. This is the legal-but-ugly half of the Type pair: a parser that gives Type blocks their own line-oriented sub-parser -- as this repo's grammar effectively does, with typeStmt_Element terminated by NEWLINE+ -- risks rejecting valid code here, which is the more damaging direction of error because it takes the whole module down.

Two Type members on one line, separated by a colon. Predicted illegal, and this is the case most likely to overturn my reasoning elsewhere: a Type member is not a statement -- it is an element of a record layout, with its own restricted syntax and its own compiler errors -- so the general statement separator has no obvious business inside the block. Assigning and printing Y makes the outcome legible if I am wrong: it prints 9 only if the member after the colon really became part of the record.

A colon joining the Type header to its first member -- the block-opener analogue of the Sub-header case, and a tighter test than joining two members. Even a compiler that accepted colons between members would still have to separately permit a block header that does not end its own line. Predicted illegal; kept distinct from the previous case so the two candidate rules ('no colons in a Type block at all' versus 'no colon after the header') can be told apart.

A continuation inside the two-word block terminator End Type. Same lexical argument as splitting Option Explicit, and the same trap for this repo's grammar, which defines END_TYPE as one token containing a literal space. Distinct from the Option case because a block terminator is matched by the block parser rather than scanned in the declarations preamble, so an implementation that handles one correctly may still not handle the other.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 1 : Invalid inside Enum Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: An Enum member whose initialiser is continued onto the next line. Predicted legal for the ordinary lexical reason, and the printed value pins down which of two failure modes a wrong implementation has: printing 3 means the continuation was joined properly, while printing 0 would mean the member was accepted with no initialiser and the stray value line swallowed -- a silent wrong answer, which is worse than a parse error.

The Enum twin of the colon-joined Type members, and predicted illegal for the same reason: an enumeration constant is a member of a block with its own syntax, not a free-standing statement. Kept as a separate case rather than assumed to follow the Type result, because an Enum member carries an expression on its right-hand side while a Type member carries a type, so the two blocks may well be parsed by different code. Prints 2 if I am wrong.

The single most consequential case in this file: the canonical multi-line Win32 Declare, broken before Lib and again before the argument list. Nearly every real VB6 module that touches the API is written this way, so a parser that mishandles it is not merely inaccurate, it is unusable. Predicted legal with high confidence. Calling the import rather than only declaring it confirms the reassembled statement was compiled correctly and not merely tolerated.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 1 : Invalid outside procedure Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: The same Declare, but the break falls inside the library-name string literal. Predicted illegal: inside a string the underscore is just a character, so no line join happens, the literal is left unterminated at the end of the physical line, and the statement is malformed. The interesting failure mode is the opposite one -- an implementation that strips continuations in a pre-pass over raw text, before it knows about string literals, will happily produce a working import of 'kernel32' and accept code the real compiler rejects.

A continuation between a keyword and the string literal it governs, rather than between two whole clauses. Distinct from the multi-line Declare above because the break lands mid-clause, where a parser that tries to resynchronise on line boundaries has the least context to work with. Predicted legal. Renaming the import to GTC makes the Alias clause load-bearing: the call only resolves if the continued string really attached to the Alias keyword.

A single Const statement declaring two constants, continued after the comma. Predicted legal: this is the shape the continuation character exists for, and the trailing comma leaves the statement obviously incomplete, so even a recovery-based parser has a clear signal. Prints 3 only if the second constant was really declared by the same statement; if the continuation were mishandled, B would be undefined and the module would fail rather than print a wrong number.

The same statement broken at a nastier point -- between the constant's name and its equals sign, so the first physical line ends with a bare identifier that would look like a complete line on its own. Unlike the comma case there is no dangling operator to signal incompleteness, which is what makes this the harder half of the pair. Predicted legal; prints 5.

The two mechanisms of this area interacting on one logical line at module level: a colon separator, then a continuation carrying the second statement onto the next physical line. Order of operations matters -- the continuation is joined by the scanner while the colon is interpreted by the parser -- so this only works if the join happens first and the resulting logical line is then split at the colon. Unsure also because it inherits whatever module-level colon rule the earlier cases establish. Prints 3 if both statements survived.

The baseline for the Attribute lines: one on its own line, ahead of the options, exactly as VB6 itself writes them when it saves a .bas file. Predicted legal for a file compiled from disk. Worth measuring anyway because Attribute has a split personality -- the VBE refuses a hand-typed Attribute line inside the editor while the file format requires it -- so a harness that feeds source through the editor and one that compiles a file may legitimately disagree here, and knowing which is being measured is needed to read the other two Attribute cases.

An Attribute line colon-joined to an ordinary directive. Predicted illegal on the grounds that Attribute is barely a statement in the language at all -- it is file-format metadata the compiler reads positionally, ahead of the code proper -- so the statement separator should not reach it. If it turns out legal, the useful consequence is that Attribute is going through the same machinery as everything else, which would also predict the next case going the same way.

The continuation counterpart to the previous case, and unsure for the reason that makes it interesting: if Attribute lines are consumed by a positional pre-scan of the file header, that scan may never have been taught about continuations, because nothing that legitimately writes these lines has ever needed one. A rare spot where the answer plausibly differs between two things that are both 'just lexing'.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 1 : Syntax error Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: A whole conditional block collapsed onto one line with colons. Predicted illegal on documented grounds rather than by guess: the language reference states the directive forms have no single-line variant and that no other code may share a line with them -- a restriction it calls out precisely because the corresponding If statement DOES have a single-line form, so a reader would otherwise assume symmetry. The Debug.Print is there so that a legal result is observable instead of silent.

A continuation inside a directive's condition -- the case where the two documented rules collide. 'No other code on the directive's line' is a rule about code, and a continuation is not code; but if directives are scanned by physical line, the continuation never gets a chance to join anything. Both readings are defensible from the reference, which is exactly why this needs measuring rather than deciding. Prints IN if it compiles at all, since the condition is true under either reading.

The same continuation question aimed at #Const rather than #If, and it separates two rules the previous case cannot. #Const is a definition, not a block opener, so the single-line prohibition the reference states for #If, #ElseIf, #Else and #End If does not name it at all. Made observable through a following #If: printing DBG proves the constant really became 1, and silence would mean the continued value never reached it -- an undefined conditional constant evaluates as Empty rather than raising an error, so this can fail quietly.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 4 : You must terminate the # If block with an # EndIf Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: The minimal violation of the directive line rule: not a statement sharing the line, just a trailing colon with nothing after it. Predicted illegal because the documented restriction is stated about the line, not about whether anything meaningful follows. Everywhere else in VB6 a trailing colon is a harmless empty statement, which makes this the sharpest available test of whether directives are policed as lines or as statements -- and it is the shape most likely to arrive from a text-processing tool rather than a human.

Every inter-token gap is a single TAB rather than a space, including the ones the grammar spells as a mandatory WS (Dim WS ident WS As WS type). The repo lexer defines WS as [ \t]+ so it should cope, but a hand-written tokenizer that special-cases the space character would reject the whole module. Expect tabs=3.
Leading indentation is tabs only, at two depths. VB6 is not layout-sensitive so indentation should be pure noise; this checks that nothing keys off column position. Expect deep.

Trailing spaces and tabs after every statement, including after Then in a block If. That one matters: whether Then is last on the line decides block form versus single-line form, so the trailing whitespace must be discarded before that test or this becomes a single-line If with an empty body plus a stray End If. Expect trail.

The statement separator is surrounded by TABs rather than spaces. A direct hit on the repo grammar, whose NEWLINE rule is WS? ('\r'? '\n' | COLON ' ') WS? -- the colon alternative demands a literal space after the colon, so a tab there is not a separator at all. Real VB6 should not care. Expect a1b2.

Why: A separator colon with nothing after it, on the very last line of the file, following End Sub -- so the empty statement it introduces would land at module level, outside any procedure. A trailing colon inside a procedure is ordinary; whether module scope tolerates the same empty statement is the open question. Differs from the covered statement-colon-End-Sub shape in that here the colon comes after End Sub.

A procedure whose entire body is one colon: a line holding only a separator, hence two empty statements and no real one. The parser must accept an empty statement as a whole block, not merely as filler between real statements.

The same lone colon, but between declarations at module level where only declarations and procedure headers are allowed. If the empty statement is manufactured by the tokenizer rather than the parser it may slip through here too; predicting illegal because module level has no statement slot to put it in.

Blank lines in every structural position at once: before the option block, between it and the procedure header, immediately after the header, before End Sub, and twice after it at end of file. Each is a separate NEWLINE+ site in the grammar, and any one of them written as exactly-one-NEWLINE would fail. Expect blanks.

The separating lines are not empty -- they hold spaces, a lone tab, and a mixture. A truly blank line and a line of invisible whitespace are different token streams (WS then newline, versus newline alone), so they are worth separating. Expect ws9.

The gap between Select Case and the first Case is the one place in VB6 where an ordinary statement is forbidden. Blank lines and comments are the documented exception, so this should compile -- but a grammar that models the gap as nothing at all, rather than as NEWLINE+, will reject it. Expect two.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 1 : Syntax error Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: A continuation followed by a wholly blank line, but with an argument list still open. Distinct from the plain blank-after-continuation case because a joiner that tracks bracket depth might keep gluing lines while a paren is unclosed. VB6 continuation is purely lexical with no bracket awareness, so the blank line should end the logical line and leave an unclosed call.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 2 : Syntax error Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: The line after the continuation contains exactly one TAB. Whether that counts as blank decides between 'x = 1 +' (incomplete, an error) and 'x = 1 + 2'. Named separately from the space-only variant because a blankness test written as a run of spaces would treat the two differently.

The file's last characters are space-underscore with no line terminator at all. The repo's LINE_CONTINUATION rule requires ' ' '_' '\r'? '\n', so at true EOF the underscore is not a continuation but a stray token after End Sub. Real VB6 must either synthesise a final newline (leaving a continuation with nothing to continue) or choke on the underscore; both are errors, so the prediction survives either reading. NB this tests what it claims only if the harness does not append a trailing newline.

The control for the case above: a well-formed module whose final End Sub has no terminating newline. The grammar's startRule ends with 'module EOF' and most inner rules are spelled NEWLINE+, so a required final newline is exactly the kind of thing a grammar acquires by accident. Expect eof. Also harness-dependent -- if the writer appends a newline this degenerates to an ordinary module.

Eight consecutive continuations in one logical line, far deeper than the two- and three-line chains elsewhere in this corpus. VB6 documents a ceiling of 25 continuations per logical line, so eight should be comfortably legal; the point is to catch a joiner with a small fixed lookahead or one stack frame per joined line. Expect chain=9.

Five 240-character literals joined by continuations: every physical line stays short but the joined logical line runs to roughly 1250 characters. VB6 documents a 1023-character line limit, and it is not clear whether that is measured per physical line (fine here) or after joining (over the limit). If legal, expect 1200.

It looks like whitespace and is not: VB6's whitespace class is space and tab, and this byte is a printable character in the ANSI codepage, so the line should read as a garbage identifier. A pass here would mean the tokenizer uses a Unicode whitespace test.

Why: A vertical tab (U+000B) doing the job of the mandatory space after Dim. It is a C-family whitespace character and an ASCII control, but VB6's own whitespace class is space and tab only. Leaning illegal, though control characters are exactly where a reader written against a C runtime's isspace would diverge from the language definition.

Why: A form feed (U+000C) alone on a line between two procedures -- the printer page-break convention older BASIC listings used. Whether VB6 treats it as whitespace, as a line terminator, or as garbage at module level is unrecorded. If legal, both procedures compile.

`For Each` is not one lexer token here - it is two keywords joined by a mandatory WS in the parser rule. A continuation is on the hidden channel, so the parser sees FOR and EACH adjacent with no WS between them and the rule cannot match. Predicting legal, on the same footing as End _ Sub: nothing in the reference distinguishes the multi-word keywords VB6 happens to lex as one token from the ones it assembles later, and a writer splitting a long For Each line has no way to know which kind they are dealing with.

Same shape as For _ Each: RESUME and NEXT are joined by a parser-level WS, not lexed as one token. Worth measuring separately because Next is also a statement in its own right, so if VB6 rejected the split it might plausibly do so by reading the second line as a stray Next rather than as a syntax error - a different diagnostic, and a different fix.

The third parser-assembled pair. Distinct from the other two because the very next line begins with Case, so a compiler that rejected the split would be choosing between 'Select is not a statement' and 'Case without Select' - and this file exists partly to find out which errors VB6 actually issues for the family.

The keyword-then-literal shape, deliberately NOT relaxed in the grammar. Unlike two adjacent keywords, `Lib` and a string literal CAN abut in the token stream with nothing between them, so 'they are adjacent, therefore something hidden separated them' is not a valid argument here and the WS could not be made optional on reasoning alone. This case is what decides it. Predicting legal - a Declare line is long and splitting it before the library name is the obvious place.

The other half of the same question, and the reason the previous case cannot simply be waved through. If VB6 accepts `Lib"kernel32"` with no separator at all, then making the WS optional is faithful; if it rejects it, then WS? would be a real widening and the fix has to admit the continuation more narrowly. Genuinely unsure: VB6 is lax about whitespace in many places and strict in a few, and I know of no rule that predicts which this is.

Alias sits in the same rule as Lib and has the same keyword-then-literal shape. Measured separately rather than assumed to follow Lib, because the two are different tokens in different positions and this corpus has already been wrong once about a rule generalising across a rule boundary.

Keyword-then-numeric-literal, and a module-level directive rather than a statement. Unsure for a reason the other cases do not have: Option lines are read by the compiler's front end before much else, and directives are exactly the kind of construct that can turn out to be line-oriented in a way ordinary statements are not. If any member of this family is illegal, this is the one.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 4 : Syntax error Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: The boundary of the fix. A continuation is hidden from the parser, and so is a comment - so a grammar that admits hidden tokens between End and Sub would admit this too. Predicting illegal: VB6 does not allow a comment on a continued line at all (it ends the statement), so this should fail regardless of the keyword split. Included because if it turns out LEGAL, the keyword separator is not the whole story.

Two continuations in a row inside the keyword. The separator either accepts a run of them or it does not, and a run is what real reformatted code produces when a line is split twice. Predicting legal by the same reasoning as one continuation, but it is a distinct grammar path - the fragment has to repeat, not merely allow one.

A split keyword inside a single-line If - the two constructs this corpus has already had to fix, interacting. The single-line If body ends at the newline, and the continuation is precisely a way of postponing that newline, so this asks whether the two agree about where the statement stops. Predicting legal, and predicting output [a]: the Exit For must still leave the loop.

A line consisting of Rem and a colon and nothing else. If Rem takes the rest of the line as text then the colon is text; if the colon separates statements then this is a comment followed by an empty statement. Both readings accept it, so the interest is in what it constrains, not whether it compiles. Predicting legal.

THE hazard case for this whole group. Widening the Rem separator risks lexing `RemX` as the keyword Rem followed by X, which would turn an assignment into a comment and silently delete the statement. VB6 must treat RemX as an ordinary identifier - if it did not, no VB6 program could name a variable Remainder. Predicting legal, and predicting it prints 5. Written to fail loudly if a fix over-reaches.

The same hazard with a digit rather than a letter after Rem, because a separator rule written as 'Rem followed by anything that is not a letter' would admit this one while excluding RemX. Measuring both is what distinguishes a rule keyed on the identifier boundary from one keyed on a character class.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 1 : Syntax error Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: Is Rem a reserved word? If it is, this fails at the Dim. Predicting illegal, but the prediction is worth little: VB6's reserved-word list is not what anyone remembers it to be, and several words that feel reserved are not. The answer decides whether the grammar may treat REM as an unconditional keyword token.

Genuinely ambiguous and genuinely useful. If Rem is a keyword the moment it is not part of a longer identifier, this is a comment reading `=1`. If Rem can be an implicitly-declared Variant, this is an assignment. If Rem is reserved AND requires a separator, it is a syntax error. Three defensible outcomes, and they need different grammars. Unsure.

No whitespace between Rem and the apostrophe. Under a separator-required rule this is not a comment at all and probably a syntax error; under a keyword-only rule the apostrophe is just the first character of the remark text. Unsure, and cheap to measure.

A keyword abutting a string literal, which the keyword-splitting work established VB6 tolerates elsewhere (Lib"kernel32" compiles). Whether that tolerance extends to Rem is a separate question - Rem is unusual in that what follows it is not a token at all but raw text.

Rem, a tab, then end of line - a bare Rem that a trailing tab has been left on, which is what a text editor produces when someone deletes a remark's text. Distinct from bare-rem-with-no-text because the separator IS present here; only the remark is empty.

The current COMMENT rule admits LINE_CONTINUATION inside the comment body, which would make the Debug.Print "B" line part of the remark and silently delete it. That is a wrong-value failure, not a late-error one, so it matters more than most. VB6's actual behaviour is undocumented here and the two candidate readings differ in what the program prints, so this needs both a legality and a behaviour measurement. Unsure.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 2 : Expected End Sub Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: The same question with the worst possible payload. If a trailing underscore extends a Rem comment onto the following line, this module has no End Sub and will not compile - which is exactly how a user would discover the behaviour, from a procedure that mysteriously will not close. Included because the failure mode is a whole module rather than one statement.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 4 : Syntax error Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: A single-line If whose entire Then branch is a comment - so the branch has no statement in it at all. The corpus already established that the joined tail after Then belongs to the branch; this asks whether a branch may be empty once the comment is removed. Unsure: an If with a genuinely empty Then is often a syntax error even where the comment form is not.

The Else half of the same question, and a real idiom - Else Rem is how a VB6 author documents a deliberately empty alternative. If this is illegal the idiom is not what I think it is, which is worth knowing either way.

A named label already carries a colon, so this should satisfy the documented 'Rem following another statement needs a colon' rule without a second colon. The corpus covers the numeric-line-number form of this but not the named-label form, and they go through different grammar rules here.

The line-number form WITH the optional colon, as the companion to the existing case that omits it. Both should be legal; measuring both is what shows the colon is optional after a line number rather than merely tolerated in one arrangement.

An empty statement between the assignment and the Rem. The colon-separator work established that a run of colons is legal; this checks that a Rem may follow one, which the grammar's COLON? prefix - matching at most ONE colon - would refuse.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 0 : Expected: identifier Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: The reserved-word question from the other side, and the one that would be genuinely nasty: if Rem may name a procedure, then a bare `Rem` on a line is ambiguous between a comment and a call. Predicting illegal. If it is legal, the bare-Rem fix needs to know which reading VB6 takes.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 0 : User-defined type without members not allowed Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: The grammar lists REM in `ambiguousKeyword`, the rule that lets a keyword act as an identifier in positions like a member name. If Rem begins a comment the moment it stands as a whole word, no such position can exist and that listing is wrong. Predicting illegal - and if it IS illegal, REM should come out of ambiguousKeyword rather than being left as a rule nothing can reach.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 2 : Enum without members not allowed Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: Rem as the ONLY enum member, which is what makes this decisive. The first version of this case listed Rem alongside a second member and compiled - and I read that as 'Rem may name an enum member', which is exactly backwards. It compiled because the Rem line VANISHED as a comment and the other member carried the enum. With Rem alone there is nothing left, so an empty-enum error proves the line is a comment. The companion UDT case says the same thing more loudly: it fails with 'User-defined type without members not allowed'.

Error: Compile Error in File 'C:\hexide-legality\Module1.bas', Line 0 : Expected: identifier Build of 'verify.exe' failed.
Why: A parameter named Rem. Included because a parameter list is the position where a reserved word most often turns out to be permitted, and because getting this wrong would make a real Declare or Sub signature unparseable.

The question the Else-Rem case raises once the comment is removed. `Else Rem x` is legal, and a comment is invisible to the parser, so the grammar can only accept it by allowing an EMPTY else body - which also accepts a bare trailing Else. Whether that is faithful or a widening depends entirely on this measurement, and I have no confident prediction: a dangling Else is the kind of thing a compiler either shrugs at or refuses outright.

The apostrophe spelling of the Else-Rem idiom. Both forms are invisible to the parser, so if these two disagree the difference cannot be syntactic and something else is going on. Predicting legal, and predicting it agrees with the Rem form - a cross-check on the reading rather than a new fact.

A colon straight after Then, with what looks like the body on the following line and no End If. The corpus already measures `If x Then: Debug.Print` (colon then body on the SAME line, legal) and `If x Then:` followed by an End If (illegal, because the colon commits VB6 to the single-line form and the End If then has no block to close). This third arrangement is the one neither covers, and HexIDE rejects it today - so if VB6 accepts it, it is a FALSE REJECTION hiding in a gap between two existing cases, which is the direction that takes a whole module down.

The control for the previous case: colon after Then with the body on the same line and no End If. Included so the pair isolates WHERE the body sits, rather than confounding it with whether an End If is present. Predicting legal.
